title: Onboarding funnel event (funnel.v1)
description: The cross-repo onboarding-funnel event contract, funnel.v1. One event is one observation of a lead moving through the onboarding funnel: {run_id, ts, stage, event, actor, outcome, meta?}. The shape is deliberately small and closed so any surface (SDK, coding agent, portal, backend) can emit a comparable event without inventing fields. This is a contract-first, pre-release schema: it defines the WIRE, not any backend route or storage, and several invariants it depends on cannot be expressed in JSON Schema and are enumerated as backend obligations rather than assumed proven. Every field is bounded above so a malformed or hostile payload is rejected by the contract rather than by downstream processing.
x-backend-obligations: Tenant/project ownership of run_id is resolved from the authenticated request context, never from a client field: an event whose run_id belongs to another tenant must be rejected at admission. The body carries no tenant field and this contract cannot check ownership.

Stage-order reconciliation across separate events: the funnel order of stages (and whether a given stage may follow another for the same run_id) is a relationship between distinct events that JSON Schema cannot compare, so ordering is reconciled server-side, not in this per-event contract.

meta total size: the 65536-byte event-body ceiling (x-max-event-bytes) is a byte count over the canonicalized event that JSON Schema cannot compute, so it is enforced backend-side at admission, not by this contract. The per-value (8192-char) and per-key (64) bounds declared here cap the obvious inflation vectors but do not add up to the byte ceiling.

meta redaction: meta is opaque user-authored content and MUST be redacted from logs, telemetry, and exports downstream. The contract bounds and classifies meta but cannot guarantee any value inside it is free of sensitive content.

Access-period linkage: an access_period_ended or access_restored event fires long after the originating onboarding attempt, so the producer must durably retain the run_id correlation; this per-event contract records observations of the period's lifecycle and never its duration, deadline, or policy, which are resolved server-side.

schema.description: Required wire self-descriptor naming this contract and version; it must be exactly 'funnel.v1'. Requiring it means every event self-identifies its contract version, so once the closed enums (stage/actor/outcome) evolve a consumer can tell a funnel.v1 event from a later version instead of silently mis-reading a versionless one. A breaking change ships a new const value rather than reinterpreting this one.

run_id.description: An opaque public correlation id for the onboarding attempt; it is not a secret and reveals nothing about credentials. It is a stable join key so events for the same attempt can be correlated across surfaces. Mechanically the pattern requires a value that both starts and ends with an ASCII letter or digit, with '.', '_', ':', '-' permitted only between alphanumerics and nothing else, so whitespace, quotes, at-signs, control characters, non-ASCII, and punctuation-only values are rejected. The end is anchored with a negative lookahead rather than '$', because under the Python validator '$' also matches immediately before a trailing newline, which would admit a value like 'lead-1\n'. That is a guarantee about SHAPE, not about meaning.

ts.description: RFC-3339 timestamp in UTC, emitted with a trailing Z. The pattern enforces the stated form rather than describing it: 'format: date-time' alone also admits a local offset (2026-07-17T13:00:00+03:00), and an offset-bearing timestamp read as UTC silently moves an event by hours, which reorders a funnel. This is a new contract with no emitters to break, so the form the prose promises is enforced; an emitter with a local clock normalizes to UTC before it emits. The fractional part is limited to at most 9 digits (nanosecond precision): a deliberate RFC-3339-UTC subset mirroring the platform's shared UtcTimestamp, so a timestamp carrying 10 or more fractional digits is outside the subset and rejected.

stage.description: The funnel stage this event observes. Closed so a consumer never has to guess what a stage means; a stage that fits no member is a versioned enum addition, not a free-text escape hatch. 'access_period_started' records the account's portal access period beginning at registration; 'access_period_ended' records that period elapsing; 'access_restored' records access being restored on the same account. 'key' records API-key issuance and is non-authorizing — a key is a credential, never the entitlement. The enum is listed in funnel order, but ORDER IS NOT ENFORCED HERE (see x-backend-obligations). A lifecycle observation of the access period carries outcome 'ok' — the observation succeeded; drop-off is not inferred from it.

event.description: A bounded, opaque event label within the stage (an identifier grammar: ASCII letters and digits, with '.', '_', ':', '/', '+', '-' permitted only between alphanumerics, so a value starts and ends with a letter or digit). Constrained to an identifier grammar rather than left free-form so it cannot become an egress channel for prose or PII. This grammar guarantees a SHAPE, not an absence of content, so a value derived from user data must still be treated as content downstream.

actor.description: Who caused this event: 'human' (the person onboarding), 'agent' (an AI coding agent acting on their behalf), or 'system' (the platform itself). Closed so the actor of every funnel step is unambiguous.

outcome.description: How this stage attempt resolved: 'ok' (succeeded), 'retry' (transient failure, will be attempted again), 'fail' (terminal failure at this stage), or 'abandon' (the lead stopped without completing). Closed so a drop-off is recorded as a value, not inferred from the absence of a later event.

meta.description: Optional opaque, user-authored annotations for this event: a bounded map of string keys to string values. Each value is capped at 8192 characters and the map at 64 keys, so no single meta value or key count is unbounded. JSON Schema cannot count the canonicalized byte size of the whole event, so the 65536-byte event ceiling (x-max-event-bytes) is NOT enforced by this schema — it is a backend obligation (see x-backend-obligations); the per-value and per-key bounds here only cap the obvious inflation vectors. meta is treated as user content: do NOT place structured platform data here, and redact it from logs and exports. The contract guarantees the container is bounded, never that any value inside it is free of sensitive content.
